newsitem.title: USA: Authorities appeal for calm in St. Petersburg.
newsitem.headline: Authorities appeal for calm in St. Petersburg.

text.p: An uneasy calm returned to a poor black neighborhood on Thursday after a night of shooting and arson set off by a grand jury's decision to clear a white policeman of killing a black youth.

As night fell, authorities appealed to residents for calm. They also increased police patrols in the city after a second bout of racial violence in less than a month, centered near the headquarters of a militant black group that has called for the execution of St. Petersburg's mayor and police chief.
The group, already under investigation by federal prosecutors for its role in last month's riots, is part of a national network known as the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement.
"We don't believe we're out of the woods yet. We've got a continuing crisis," Police Chief Darrel Stephens said.

Police and some city officials blamed Wednesday's violence on small, roving bands of youths and said unlike the spontaneous violence of last month, Wednesday's shootings and arson appeared to have been orchestrated.

The violence spilled from a confrontation at the simple, two-floor headquarters of the Uhuru group in south St. Petersburg. Stephens said the police department's strategy had been to arrest key members of the movement to get them off the streets when the violence was threatened, thereby removing potential threats and tempering community reaction.

In all, three members of the group were arrested on Wednesday on outstanding warrants for minor traffic offenses. A crowd gathered at the building after police arrested one man and officers clashed with other group members.
In a fiery meeting early on Thursday at City Hall, some city council members questioned why the police, well aware of the group's threats, had not acted sooner.
"I'm furious," said councilwoman Connie Kone. "We're sitting here on the sidelines like a bunch of bimbos."
Over 100 fires were set, destroying at least a dozen homes and businesses and causing at least $1 million in damage.
City officials said they had arrested 11 people as a result of the violence on Wednesday night and another person, a girl, on Thursday in connection with a fire.
Cynthia Moore, 30, returned to her childhood home on Thursday morning to find it virtually burned to the ground, a bit of charred wood frame still standing.

"What did whoever did this get out of it?" Moore asked as she looked at the rubble of the uninsured home her family owned for more than 30 years. "They didn't get nothing out of it. It ain't changed a thing."

Responding to complaints from residents that fire crews did not answer calls, St. Petersburg Fire chief Jim Callahan said at a news conference Thursday that his crews were slow to respond to some fires because of the violence in the streets.
"It's really beyond our control. We can't get into an area under gunfire, rocks, bricks," he said.

At least seven people were hurt in the melee, including a police officer shot in the leg and another in a helicopter grazed by a bullet. Three civilians were treated for gunshot wounds and two firefighters were hurt.
Police used tear gas to disperse angry crowds of youths, sparking charges from some neighborhood residents that the authorities had started the trouble.

"They (police) made this riot happen last night," said a 25-year-old woman who asked not to be identified. "They didn't let our young men speak. If they wouldn't have shot that tear gas, none of this would have happened."

The grand jury's action outraged the black community. The panel, which included one black member, decided that officer James Knight was justified in shooting Tyron Lewis, 18, on the night of Oct. 24. The shooting set off a night of rioting in which 11 people were hurt and 30 businesses and homes torched.

The Coalition of African American Leadership, a moderate group, said it was considering a variety of measures in protest, including an economic boycott, a civil lawsuit and peaceful marches. A federal civil rights investigation of last month's shooting is under way.
The Uhuru group, named after a Swahili word for "freedom," recently held a mock trial at which "judges" decided the city's police chief and mayor were guilty of murder and should be executed.

The local group has about 100 members and is led by Joe Waller, a former member of the Black Panthers. The group is part of a national network and was founded in 1991. Shortly after the grand jury decision, the group handed out fliers for an evening meeting that urged black citizens to organize against being "shot down in the streets like dogs."
